endorsements.quote: Decisions made to change use context or the targeted population outside the intended or initially evaluated use can alter the effectiveness of the algorithm and require reevaluation.

endorsements.title: Feasibility-First Risk Management for Clinical AI: A Deterministic Systems Intelligence Framework for Release, Monitoring, Rollback and Withholding
endorsements.quote: Active monitoring is a heightened state for tools whose use is allowed but whose risk profile requires intensified surveillance. Triggers may include a new site, a new population, a changed electronic health record workflow, borderline subgroup performance, early drift signals or uncertainty about downstream behaviour.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven sources endorse re-evaluating an AI tool before its use, population, setting, or indication changes, but no supplied study tests whether such re-evaluation prevents harm or performance loss. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory guidance rather than empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no supplied study documents the hazard. Support comes from five frameworks and guidance documents at must or should strength, one framework that describes the practice, and one commentary. The NIST passage concerns consent withdrawal and does not address scope changes, so it adds little direct support.

FDA guidance on predetermined change control plans states that modifications must keep a device within its intended use. This suggests that expanding use beyond that scope falls outside a cleared change plan. The guidance gives the recommendation a regulatory anchor for AI tools that are regulated as devices.

The CHAI playbooks propose routing material changes in scope, configuration, or intended use back through intake or risk categorization. A commentary lists a new site, a new population, or a changed electronic health record workflow as triggers for heightened monitoring. Neither source reports how often such triggers are detected in practice or what the review costs.

The radiology multi-society statement advises proceeding with great caution, if at all, when a tool tested only on adults is considered for pediatric use. This describes a plausible failure mode, but no supplied study measures how often expansion without review leads to errors that reach patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares tools expanded with and without formal re-evaluation, measures performance change after expansion to new sites or populations, or estimates the staff time and delay that re-evaluation adds. Studies are also needed on how governance bodies detect informal scope changes when clinicians begin using a tool outside its evaluated context.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Expansion to such populations may be a case where untested performance differs, and the absence of data leaves health systems without guidance on what a re-evaluation for these groups should include.
